questions.text: How many moles of oxygen atoms are present in 4.4 g of CO₂? (Molar mass of CO₂ = 44 g mol⁻¹)

options.why: 0.1 mol is the amount of CO₂ molecules, not O atoms.
Doubled twice — each CO₂ has 2 O atoms, so 0.1 × 2 = 0.2.
Divided by the number of atoms instead of multiplying.

questions.explanation: n(CO₂) = 4.4 / 44 = 0.1 mol. Each molecule has 2 O atoms, so n(O) = 0.2 mol.

questions.text: 2 g of H₂ is reacted with 32 g of O₂ to form water (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). What mass of water is formed?

options.why: Treated O₂ as limiting; H₂ (1 mol) runs out first.
Added reactant masses — O₂ is in excess and 16 g of it remains.
Halved the moles of water; 1 mol H₂ gives 1 mol H₂O.

questions.explanation: n(H₂) = 1 mol, n(O₂) = 1 mol. 1 mol H₂ needs only 0.5 mol O₂, so H₂ is limiting and gives 1 mol H₂O = 18 g.

questions.text: What volume of 0.1 M KMnO₄ is required to completely oxidise 50 mL of 0.5 M FeSO₄ in acidic medium?

options.why: Ignored the 1 : 5 MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ stoichiometry (n-factor 5 vs 1).
Decimal slip in litres → mL: 0.005 mol / 0.1 M = 0.05 L = 50 mL.
Used 0.2 M for KMnO₄ instead of the given 0.1 M.

questions.text: What is the maximum number of electrons that can have n = 3 and l = 2?

options.why: 18 is the capacity of the whole n = 3 shell, not the 3d subshell.
5 is the number of 3d orbitals; each holds 2 electrons.
6 is the capacity of a p subshell (l = 1).

questions.explanation: l = 2 is a d subshell with 2l + 1 = 5 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons → 10.

questions.text: The energy of the electron in the second Bohr orbit of He⁺ is (E₁ for H = −13.6 eV):

options.why: Forgot the Z² factor — that is the value for hydrogen.
Used n = 1 instead of the second orbit.
Multiplied by Z instead of Z².

questions.text: The first line of the Balmer series of hydrogen has λ = 656 nm. What is λ for the first Balmer line of Li²⁺?

options.why: Used 1/λ ∝ Z instead of Z².
Multiplied by Z²; wavelength is inversely proportional to Z².
Divided by 4 instead of Z² = 9.

questions.explanation: 1/λ ∝ Z² for the same transition, so λ(Li²⁺) = 656 / 9 ≈ 72.9 nm.

questions.concept: First law: ΔU in isothermal processes
questions.text: For the isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas, the change in internal energy ΔU is:

options.why: Heat absorbed equals work done; U of an ideal gas depends only on T.
That expression is q (= −w), not ΔU.

options.text: Negative, since the gas does work
options.why: True for an adiabatic expansion — the question says isothermal.

questions.explanation: For an ideal gas U depends only on temperature. Isothermal ⇒ ΔT = 0 ⇒ ΔU = 0.

questions.text: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) at 300 K, the value of ΔH − ΔU is (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹):

options.why: Sign error — Δn₍g₎ = 2 − 4 = −2.
Took Δn₍g₎ = −1; there are 4 mol of gaseous reactants.
Counted only H₂; Δn₍g₎ = moles of gaseous products − reactants.

questions.text: A reaction has ΔH = +30 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Above what temperature does it become spontaneous?

options.why: kJ and J not reconciled — convert ΔH to 30 000 J first.
Extra factor of 10 in the unit conversion.
With ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG < 0 at high T.

questions.text: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the relation between Kp and Kc is:

options.why: Sign of Δn₍g₎ flipped; Δn₍g₎ = −2.
Only true when Δn₍g₎ = 0.
Δn₍g₎ is products − reactants = 2 − 4 = −2.

questions.text: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at equilibrium, an inert gas is added at constant volume. The equilibrium:

options.why: That is the constant-pressure case; here the volume is fixed.
Partial pressures of reacting species are unchanged.
K changes only with temperature.

questions.explanation: At constant volume, concentrations / partial pressures of reactants and products do not change, so Q = K and nothing shifts.

questions.text: 2 mol of HI is placed in a 1 L flask. At equilibrium (2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂), 0.4 mol of H₂ is present. What is Kc?

options.why: Subtracted 0.4 from HI; 2 mol HI is consumed per mol H₂ formed.
Forgot to square [HI] in the denominator.
Wrote Kc for the reverse reaction H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI.

questions.text: Which carbocation is the most stable?

options.why: That is the least stable — no hyperconjugation.
Primary: only 3 α-H for hyperconjugation.
Secondary: 6 α-H, fewer than tertiary.

questions.explanation: Tertiary carbocation has 9 α-hydrogens for hyperconjugation and +I from three methyl groups.

questions.text: Which of the following is the strongest acid?

options.why: −I effect is cumulative; three Cl beat two.
Only one −I group stabilising the carboxylate.
That is the weakest acid of the set.

questions.explanation: Three Cl atoms exert the strongest −I effect, best stabilising the carboxylate anion.

questions.text: Which is the strongest base in aqueous solution?

options.why: Gas-phase order; in water, poor solvation of the 3° ammonium ion lowers basicity.
The lone pair is delocalised into the ring — aniline is a weak base.
No +I alkyl groups — weaker than the methylamines.

questions.explanation: In water, +I effect, solvation and steric factors balance out to make the 2° amine (CH₃)₂NH the strongest base.
